candidates.topic: Castrato Singers — The Price of a Perfect Voice
candidates.teaser: The most celebrated voices in 18th-century Europe belonged to boys who paid an unimaginable price to sing.
candidates.video_title: The Darkest Secret Behind History's Greatest Singers
candidates.video_description: For over 200 years, Europe's most celebrated opera singers were castrati — boys surgically altered before puberty to preserve their vocal range. The practice was widespread, socially accepted, and utterly brutal. The last known castrato, Alessandro Moreschi, died in 1922 and left behind actual recordings.
candidates.script: The most famous singers in 18th-century Europe weren't men or women — they were boys who had been surgically altered before puberty so their voices would never break. Thousands underwent the procedure every year, most dying in poverty after their voices faded. Only a handful became stars. The last one died in 1922 — and left behind recordings. You can still hear him today. Does that change how beautiful it sounds?

candidates.topic: The Saiga Antelope Mass Death — 200,000 in Three Days
candidates.teaser: In 2015, one of nature's most bizarre and terrifying mass die-offs wiped out half a species in just three days.
candidates.video_title: Half a Species Vanished in 3 Days — No One Knew Why
candidates.video_description: In May 2015, over 200,000 saiga antelopes — more than half the world's entire population — dropped dead within 72 hours across the Kazakh steppe. Calves died first, then mothers. Scientists were baffled for years. The cause, when finally found, was more disturbing than anyone expected.
candidates.script: In May 2015, 200,000 antelopes dropped dead in a single week — more than half the species alive on Earth. Mothers and calves collapsed within hours of each other across the Kazakh steppe. Scientists flew in from around the world and found no predator, no poison, no sign of disease spreading from outside. The killer had come from within the animals themselves. A bacterium that lives harmlessly in their throats had suddenly turned lethal. What made it snap? Scientists still aren't entirely sure.

candidates.topic: The Tungsten Filament — Why Light Bulbs Are Designed to Burn Out
candidates.teaser: The first light bulb ever made lasted 100 years — so why does yours die in a few months?
candidates.video_title: Light Bulbs Could Last Forever — So Why Don't They?
candidates.video_description: The Centennial Bulb in Livermore, California has been burning almost continuously since 1901. Engineers have known how to make near-indestructible bulbs for over a century. In 1924, the world's largest light bulb manufacturers secretly met and agreed to limit bulb lifespan to 1,000 hours. It was one of history's first documented planned obsolescence cartels.
candidates.script: There's a light bulb in California that has been switched on since 1901 — over 120 years. Engineers have always known how to build bulbs that last essentially forever. In 1924, the world's biggest bulb manufacturers held a secret meeting and agreed to cap bulb lifespan at 1,000 hours. They called it the Phoebus Cartel. It was one of history's first organized planned obsolescence schemes. Every bulb you've ever replaced may trace back to that one meeting.

candidates.topic: The Hum — A Sound Only 2% of People Can Hear
candidates.teaser: Thousands of people worldwide hear a low, constant hum that no microphone can detect — and it's slowly driving them mad.
candidates.video_title: A Sound That's Driving People Insane — No One Else Hears It
candidates.video_description: Across the world, in places like Taos, New Mexico and Bristol, England, a small percentage of residents report hearing a persistent, low-frequency hum that no recording equipment can pick up. Sufferers describe it as a diesel engine idling outside. It causes sleep deprivation, nausea, and anxiety. Decades of investigation have never produced a definitive source.
candidates.script: In Taos, New Mexico, roughly 2% of residents hear a low, constant rumbling — like a truck idling just outside. It never stops. No microphone has ever recorded it. Sufferers lose sleep, develop anxiety, some have moved cities to escape it. The same phenomenon has appeared in Bristol, Auckland, and dozens of other towns. Scientists have investigated for decades and still have no agreed explanation. If you can't hear it, you're in the majority. But the ones who do say they'd give anything to make it stop.

candidates.topic: Fatal Familial Insomnia — The Disease That Stops You Sleeping Forever
candidates.teaser: There is a real disease where sufferers slowly lose the ability to sleep — and it always ends the same way.
candidates.video_title: The Rare Disease That Steals Sleep — Then Takes Everything
candidates.video_description: Fatal Familial Insomnia is a prion disease that progressively destroys the thalamus — the brain region that regulates sleep. Patients begin with mild insomnia, rapidly escalate to total inability to sleep, then experience hallucinations, dementia, and death — all within 12 to 18 months. Only about 50 families in the world carry the mutation, and there is currently no cure.
candidates.script: There is a disease where patients slowly lose the ability to sleep — and no medication on Earth can help. It begins with mild insomnia, then within weeks the patient stops sleeping entirely. Hallucinations follow. Then dementia. Death comes within 18 months of the first symptom. It's called Fatal Familial Insomnia, and only around 50 families worldwide carry the gene. There is no treatment. No cure. Scientists are racing to find one — but so far, every night for those families carries a different kind of weight.
